title: Squared Deviations
story: A greenhouse sensor logs how far each reading is from the ideal temperature: negative for too cold, positive for too warm. The log is sorted from lowest to highest, for example [-7, -3, 0, 2, 5].
The climate system punishes big misses more, so its cost is the square of each deviation. It wants those costs sorted from smallest to largest.
task: Write squaredSorted(deviations). Return a new list with the square of every number, sorted from smallest to largest.
Aim for a single pass over the list, and use the fact that the input is already sorted.
constraints: deviations is sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: The squares in input order are 49, 9, 0, 4, 25. Sorted, they are 0, 4, 9, 25, 49. The biggest squares come from the two ends of the input, -7 and 5.
The squares in input order are 16, 1, 0, 9, 100. The largest, 100, comes from the right end, and the next largest, 16, comes from the left end.

hints: Squaring breaks the sorted order. Where in the input do the largest squares come from?
The biggest square is always at one end: the most negative or the most positive number. The middle holds the numbers closest to zero.
So build the answer from largest to smallest, taking the bigger end square each time.
Put left and right pointers at the ends and fill the result from the back. Each step, write the larger end square at the current back position and move that pointer inward.
bruteForce: Square every number and then sort the result. This is correct and takes only a few lines.
The sort costs O(n log n) and ignores that the input was already sorted, which tells you where the big values are.

walkthrough: The largest square is always at an end, so fill the answer from the back.
1. The ends are -7 and 5. Since 49 > 25, slot 4 gets 49 and left moves to -3.
• The ends are -3 and 5. Since 9 < 25, slot 3 gets 25 and right moves to 2.
• The ends are -3 and 2. Since 9 > 4, slot 2 gets 9 and left moves to 0.
• The ends are 0 and 2. Since 0 < 4, slot 1 gets 4 and right moves to 0.
• Both pointers are on 0, so slot 0 gets 0. The result is [0, 4, 9, 25, 49].
Each step places one value and moves one pointer, so the loop runs n times.
solution.timeWhy: A single loop places one value in each step.
solution.spaceWhy: The result list takes n slots, and the only other storage is the two pointers.
solution.takeaway: When a sorted input gets scrambled in a predictable way, look at the ends. Two pointers that start at the ends and fill the answer from the back merge the two sorted halves (the negative numbers and the non-negative numbers) in one pass.
